## Characters' careers

Careers beyond hiring are largely built (see `docs/DESIGN-NOTES.md`): captives can be ransomed or released, a king can dismiss a servant, and servants give notice at the end of their term, when owed back pay, or decline a hire for a better offer. A character's employment history is decided as part of his past ("A past before the game, then a past made in play"), and background checks already find dismissals among its blemishes. Decided 19 October 2026: captives can be exchanged between courts, since every good can be traded, and a character may quit out of loyalty to another court. Characters serve by contract, so quitting before the term ends breaks it: the break is recorded in his past, where background checks can find it, and back pay already owed is still paid only if he stands at that court again (from item 11a, jobs with a fee replace wages and back pay: "Jobs, not wages" in the main tab).

**Errands, not roles** (decided 18 October 2026). Characters have no fixed position or career. A king sends a person somewhere to do something, and the "role" is only what that errand happens to be. The same people are already sent as envoys or posted as spies. To keep code deciding facts, an errand is a destination plus a few things to do there, from a set the engine can carry out:

- deliver a letter, a tablet or gold;
- observe a court, a province or an army;
- carry a candidate an offer, or check a claim ("did Babylon really offer him 30?");
- pay or collect a ransom;
- buy a city or bribe someone;
- stay and report, as a resident or a spy;
- take command of an army.

A free-text mandate guides the character's judgement along the way. One errand may chain several stops, so one trusted man can go to Babylon, check a claim, deliver gold to Mitanni and come home, every leg taking time on the road. Each person is better at some work than others, but the king learns that only through checks, reputation and results. A brilliant negotiator handed an army is a gamble he may not know he is taking. A character is a set of skills, not a profession (21 October 2026): a king chooses whom to send by how competent he judges him at the work and how badly he needs it done, and a character may hold several errands at once where they overlap, such as an envoy carrying other people's tablets along his road, or a merchant who sells what he overheard in Byblos. Each extra errand is one more employer he can betray for another.

**Messengers are errands (decided 21 October 2026).** Word from abroad needs someone to carry it. A report or letter from an envoy, a spy or anyone else comes home only with a carrier: someone hired ("Anyone can hire anyone"), a traveller going that way, such as a merchant carrying letters on the side, or the person himself travelling home. Nothing arrives by itself. Carrying is an errand like any other (deliver a letter or a tablet, bring back a reply), so the messenger needs no role of his own.

- **Envoy or messenger.** An envoy has a mandate and an audience and can bargain. A messenger only delivers and brings back an answer: cheaper and quicker to find, but with no authority, so a king chooses between them for each errand. The sources draw the same line: Arzawa's king would not trust what Pharaoh's messenger said until a tablet confirmed it.
- **Word from abroad is a decision.** An envoy kept waiting or detained must choose how to get word home ("they are holding me", "the king asks for more", "shall I seal?"): hire someone at that court, trust a passing merchant, or send one of his own people. A spy's report needs a carrier too, so every report carries risk: the carrier can be intercepted, questioned or bribed, and lead back to the spy.
- **The carrier has motives of his own.** He can read what he carries if he knows its language, sell what it says, swap it for a forgery ("Swapped tablets"), lose it to bandits on the road, or deliver it faithfully because his name is his living. These are errors with motives, as pillar 3 asks.
- **No faceless channel (decided 21 October 2026).** Nothing is sent without someone, not even more slowly and with a greater chance of loss. Everything that can happen to a letter comes from its carrier, so a lost tablet is a story with someone to blame, bribe or suspect, not a roll of the dice. History had no such channel either: every letter went with someone, which is why kings complained of their messengers being held for years at a foreign court. The reason in the game is language: a tablet must be accompanied by talk. A letter was read aloud at court, and its bearer was questioned, said what the tablet left unsaid and took the answer home; the tablet confirmed the words, and the bearer spoke them ("Envoy or messenger"). Soldiers and porters do not speak the language of a foreign court and are not received by its king, so an army or a caravan can carry goods but never a letter. Handing over goods needs no language: this for that can be done by gesture, as in the silent trade Herodotus describes. Bargaining is talk, which is why a caravan only delivers what its orders say and a character leading it can strike a bargain. A letter is communication, which needs language and reading, and that is where betrayal comes in; and how well a bearer is understood follows the language system ("Languages"). Inside a realm, orders and reports travel with the realm's own couriers, men in a unit like caravans rather than named characters, since they speak the realm's own language ("Distance inside your own realm").
- **Side jobs on the road.** Those in a city see who has arrived there, so anyone may offer a passing traveller a fee to carry a tablet, and the offer wakes him ("Characters sleep like kings" below): at most one call at a stop where someone wants something. A stranger is slow, since he keeps his own road and schedule; unreliable, since he owes the sender nothing; and cheap, since he is paid for a favour on his way, not for a journey of his own. An envoy who carries for others serves two masters: Egypt's envoy taking Aziru's letter to Hatti can open it or sell it to his own king, so envoys on the road are among the best sources of intelligence in the game, and senders must choose their carriers with care. A well-paid delivery off his road delays his king's mission, and the king learns of it only when the news reaches him: he can notice side jobs, not forbid them, as with skimming.
- **Paid on delivery.** Half now and the rest from the recipient is the natural safeguard. Nothing enforces it, so it rests on reputation, like every other debt.
- **Forgery needs a skill; betrayal does not.** Most carriers cannot read Akkadian, so a passing merchant can rarely falsify what he carries, but he can sell it to someone who can, or pay a scribe to read it. The road is where the risk lies: in EA 8 Burna-Buriash complains to Pharaoh that his merchants were robbed and killed in Canaan, and asks for redress.
- **The rest emerges.** Fees, speed and trust come out of play: a carrier known for delivering faithfully can ask more, merchants on busy roads carry letters cheaply, and relay stations (build order item 15) make carriers faster.
- **Every seat uses it.** Script envoys and spies decide when to send word and whom to trust with it, and script carriers decide by their traits whether to read, sell or swap what they carry ("Every feature is every seat's").

In build order item 7 news already travels with people along the route; until item 11b, a report travels that route by itself, as if the engine carried it. From item 11b, when anyone can hire anyone, it needs a real carrier.

**Characters sleep like kings (decided 21 October 2026).** Characters follow the kings' rule ("Decided: sleep is the default" and "No triggers of the seat's own", under Pacing in the main tab), so model calls follow events, not the number of characters, and a larger pool stays affordable. After taking his errands, a character sleeps until the engine wakes him:

- an errand is finished, or can no longer be done (the road is cut, his employer has fallen);
- an offer reaches him: work, a bribe, someone wanting to buy his cargo or the tablet he carries;
- trouble: he is stopped, robbed or captured, or a band or pirates stand on his route;
- a letter or messenger addressed to him arrives;
- news that concerns him directly, such as war on his route or his employer's death, and only when that news reaches him, so a fallen capital wakes people in waves, at the speed of travel.

His errands may carry conditions in the same engine-checkable vocabulary as a king's scheduled orders ("sell in Ugarit unless the price has fallen; otherwise go on to Alashiya"), but conditions decide what he does, never when he wakes. He sets no triggers of his own: the kings' simulations showed that a seat given a way to wake itself uses it every season, and a merchant in Byblos does not know Ugarit's prices until someone tells him. A character without work sleeps until an offer reaches him. The kings' hidden safety cap applies to characters too, each request tells him how long he slept and why he woke, and his rules say what the kings' rulebook says: you are woken only when something concerns you, so plan as if these errands must carry you until then. Built in item 8, with characters as agents in local play; the engine's full set of errands comes with item 10 ("Errands, not roles").

**A life of their own.** Out of service, characters keep acting, run by scripts, so they cost no model calls:

- **Selling what they know.** A free character carries news from the courts and roads it has passed, and offers it at a price it sets (see "Characters as sellers of news").
- **Seeking work.** It travels to courts that are hiring, or to where its sympathy lies, and pitches there.
- **Going outlaw.** A character who turns outlaw may lead a band, giving the Habiru and pirates a face ("Turning outlaw" and "The way back"). Its traits shape the band: a greedy chief robs, an ambitious one wants a city. A band with a known leader can be hired as mercenaries, bribed to look elsewhere, sponsored against a rival, or hunted.

Chosen direction (18 October 2026). This ties several ideas together: generalist characters, news as an asset, outlaws as a world force, and promotion of minor actors. Scheduled in item 11; commanders come with item 13.

**A living pool.** Today all 18 characters exist from the start, nobody new appears, and the pool only shrinks (an executed spy is gone for good). In longer games with many roles, the pool needs to live:

- **Arrivals come through doors (decided 21 October 2026).** Nobody appears out of the ground. A new character enters the map through a door, a place where a route from beyond the map comes in: the western sea from Keftiu and Ahhiyawa, landing on Arzawa's coast, at Alashiya, Ugarit and Egypt; the eastern road from Elam's lands beyond Susa; the Gulf from Magan; the Red Sea from Punt; and the Nile beyond Nubia. Which places are doors is map data, at least wherever an edge market will sit ("Edge markets"), and each door's share of arrivals follows its traffic: a first guess in item 11a, then the edge markets' trade once they are built. Most arrivals are strangers from beyond the map, who take their names from that land's attested names (Linear B for the Aegeans) and their languages from it ("Who speaks what"), so each door brings its own mix, set as data from the history pass: the eastern road and the Gulf, which traded into Babylonia, bring more men with some Akkadian; the western sea brings Aegeans who mostly speak only their own tongue, the traders among them a little of the port's; the southern doors bring mostly strangers with no court's tongue. Some are locals coming home, an Egyptian back from Punt, a Babylonian merchant back from Elam, an Ugaritan back from Keftiu, with their own court's language and the edge's. From the door a newcomer travels like any character, needing passage and taking real seasons, towards wherever his skills and languages pay best ("Where characters are, and what they speak"), so whoever holds a door sees its newcomers first, as Egypt sees Nubia's; item 18 checks that courts far from every door are not starved. A stranger with no court's language still has the work that needs none: trading, carrying wares, working for himself, leading a band at sea. He learns a language by living somewhere, Luwian at Arzawa or Akkadian at Ugarit, and grows into a servant over the years. That is the Sherden's road: they appear as fighting men in Rib-Hadda's letters from Byblos, and the king of Alashiya complains that men of Lukka seize villages in his land year by year (EA 38).
- **Or they rise from the crowd.** The one door inside the map: a man the world already holds becomes someone wherever men act together without a head, a crowd of loose men, a band whose leader has fallen, mutineers, a broken army, a revolt or a fallen court's refugees ("A head rises where men lack one"). He was there all along, uncounted; now he matters. Idrimi was one, a prince of Aleppo who fled, lived among the Habiru and became king of Alalakh ("Idrimi, the outlaw who became king" in the main tab). This door opens only where its people are, so in peace nearly every newcomer is a stranger, and in war the land supplies its own desperate men. The two doors answer different things: strangers come when the pool is short ("A baseline, not a limit"), each drawn from the seeded stream by the doors' traffic ("Deterministic"), while a head rises when men need one, whatever the pool's size.
- **Who they are (decided 21 October 2026).** A newcomer is data first, like every character: the engine draws his facts and the narrator writes his persona from them once. The facts are his origin and door; why he came, from a mix that fits the door (trade, flight, a feud, soldiering, wanderlust); what he carries; his languages; and, for a man risen from the crowd, how he rose. Names come from the attested names of his land, or, where none survive, from a style the history pass sets, marked as invented. One rule keeps the stories honest: beyond the map a backstory may say anything, since nothing on the map can check it or depends on it, while on the map it says only what happened. "He fled a blood feud on Keftiu" is free; "the king of Ugarit owes him" needs a debt tablet. Origins are weighted by distance, as people travelled then: most come from just beyond the edge, Aegeans, highlanders from beyond Susa, men from beyond Nubia, and few from far away. The rarest is a man from the tin lands, since tin crossed Iran from hand to hand and almost nobody made the whole journey: he speaks nothing anyone knows, and he can tell the kings what they never knew, where tin comes from, which changes nothing they can do, since the map ends where their world ended. The western sea also brings the peoples later called the Sea Peoples. Some are already in the letters: the Sherden, fighting men at Byblos, who come through the western door with a homeland as unknown as it still is; and the Lukka, raiding Alashiya (EA 38), and the land of Danuna, named from Tyre (EA 151), which lie on or near the map, so their men come from the crowd or the nearest door. The rest, the Shekelesh, Teresh, Peleset, Tjeker and Weshesh, are first named 140 to 170 years later, under Merneptah and Ramesses III, but a people is older than its first record, so they come too, rarely, as adventurers and soldiers for hire rather than invaders, under their later names, marked in the data as first recorded later. Their age of invasion belongs to a later scenario, as Ahhiyawa as a player does.
- **Natural losses.** Battle, execution, murder, the road, plague or famine, as in "No age in this game" (plague today only kills a unit), so arrivals replace losses rather than inflate the pool. Nobody dies of old age ("No age in this game" below).
- **Deterministic.** Arrivals and deaths draw from their own seeded random stream, so existing seeds keep their characters and replays stay exact.

**No age in this game (decided 21 October 2026).** Characters have no age, and nobody dies of old age. A median game lasts about fifteen years and most under thirty, so old age would be a minor cause of death; without it, a character dies only of risk: battle, execution, murder, the road, plague or famine. Personas describe experience, such as a seasoned envoy or a new scribe, never an age or a nearing end, because a model told it is old reasons as if it will die soon. Heirs, and the generations they need, are left to a game that spans them.

**Attested characters (decided 21 October 2026).** Characters are real people of the period wherever the sources allow, such as the envoys Mane and Keliya, and every other name follows its region's attested names, from the people dossier ("Grounded in the sources").

- **The core comes from the sources.** An attested person's traits are set from what the sources tell of him: Mane, the pharaoh's envoy held for years by Tushratta, or a scribe known from his tablets. Each game varies them a little, by a seeded amount within a narrow band (a first guess of about 10 points either way on the 0–100 scale), so the essence holds while no game is the same.
- **The persona carries it.** The narrator writes each attested character's persona once from his traits and what the sources say, and it stays short, since characters are played by a smaller model with a small budget per call. It describes who he was and how he tends to act, never what history did with him, so the game can go its own way.
- **Stakes still decide.** Traits shape his strategy, as for everyone ("Stakes, not dispositions"); the sources give his starting character, not a script.
- **Kings and vassal rulers** are seats, not characters, and are grounded the same way: their temperaments by default follow what the letters show of them (the balance pass's historical archetypes).
- **Everyone else** is generated: arrivals, and the ordinary people the pool needs, take names from their region's attested names and are marked as generated in the data.
- **Nubians in Egypt's service (decided 21 October 2026).** Nubia is Egypt's own land, so Egypt's starting characters include Nubians: captains of Nubian troops above all, since Nubian soldiers garrisoned Canaan (the men who broke into Abdi-Heba's house, EA 287) and Rib-Hadda begs again and again for troops of Meluhha, the letters' name for Nubia; and the Egyptianised elite, princes raised in Pharaoh's nursery. Hekanefer, prince of Miam, a child of the royal nursery shown later in the tomb of Huy, Tutankhamun's viceroy of Kush, is a candidate for an attested character if the history pass finds that his dates fit 1346. Many such men bore Egyptian names, which is true to them. They speak Egyptian, at a skill set by background, and a Nubian tongue that no court reads but that lets them talk with Nubians from the crowd and from beyond the Nile door, and bridge for them. More Nubians come from Nubia's own crowd and through that door ("Arrivals come through doors", "A head rises where men lack one").

Built with the first character package (build order item 10), from the dossiers of item 6+.

**Enough people, not enough good ones.** The pool must be large enough to staff what the kings need: their armies, envoys and spies. If people are short now and then, kings must bid against each other, which is a good dynamic; chronic shortage at every court is not. The way to get both: plenty of ordinary people, few excellent ones. A king can nearly always find someone; competition is for talent, such as the able general or the trusted envoy. How many people there are is set by a baseline the pool keeps near, not by demand, and the price of the scarce ones by fees (the entries below).

**A baseline, not a limit (decided 21 October 2026).** The starting world, with all its courts, sets the baseline, and it does not shrink as powers fall: a conqueror has fewer rivals bidding against him, but more provinces to govern and more armies to lead, so the world's demand for people stays roughly the same through a game. One effect to watch, not to fix: the realm's own couriers carry its orders, so a bigger empire needs no more characters for its messages, and late games may have a surplus of characters, which means cheap men and more outlaws, and suits the age. The pool therefore keeps near a baseline set from the world, as a population keeps near what its land can carry ("How many characters" below). Below the baseline, arrivals come more often, through the doors ("Arrivals come through doors" above); above it, more rarely. Losses are only natural ones: battle, execution, murder, the road, plague or famine; nobody dies of old age ("No age in this game"). Nobody is removed to meet the number, so the pool is sometimes short and sometimes in surplus, and both are part of the game. City-states becoming powers (build order item 11+) do raise it ("How many characters").

**How many characters (decided 21 October 2026).** About 60 at the start, as a first guess and a setting of the table, like the end cap. The count comes from the work under way at once with seven powers and the planned map: envoys (two or three per power, 15–20), spies (one or two per power, 7–14), commanders (one per field army, 12–18), merchants and carriers on the main trade routes (the coast, the Nile, the tin road along the Euphrates, the crossings to Alashiya, the Gulf, and overland from Hatti into Syria; 10–15), band leaders, pirates and outlaws (5–8), and enough free people that hiring stays possible (10–15). That is about 60–90, and fewer in practice, since one character holds several errands ("Errands, not roles"). The characters' own calls follow their wake-ups ("Characters sleep like kings"), so what limits the number lies elsewhere:

- **The kings' view.** Every character a king knows adds to every one of his calls, on the dearest model, so a king sees only the characters he has dealt with or heard of, and his view does not grow with the pool. A human player likewise follows only those he knows, so each court still deals with a cast of known figures.
- **Waves of wake-ups.** A great event wakes everyone it touches as its news arrives; that spike, not the average, is what to watch.

Item 8 measures wake-ups per character and calls per season once characters are agents; item 18 sets the default from them. At item 11+, when some twenty city-states become powers that write letters, the pool is recounted and grows with them; their rulers get no households of their own, since nothing yet gives kin a motive. A power's starting staff follows its size, so a great king starts with more servants than a city-state.
